nameStory: American spikenard gets its name from the spike-like clusters of tiny flowers that bloom along its stems, resembling the ancient aromatic spice called "nard" from biblical times. The plant was also called "life-of-man" by early settlers, perhaps because its thick, gnarly roots were thought to have medicinal properties that could extend one's years. Indigenous peoples knew it as "Indian root" for its traditional uses.
description: American spikenard is a tall, leafy woodland plant that looks almost tropical with its large, compound leaves and branching flower clusters. This impressive herbaceous perennial grows 3-6 feet tall, creating bold patches in shaded forest areas. Despite its substantial size and lush appearance, it dies back completely each winter, re-emerging fresh each spring from thick underground roots. The plant has an overall bushy, shrub-like appearance during the growing season.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Enormous compound leaves that can span 2-3 feet across, divided into many oval leaflets with pointed tips and serrated edges. The leaves feel smooth but substantial, and are arranged alternately on thick, often reddish stems.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or greenish-white flowers arranged in multiple rounded clusters that branch out like an upside-down umbrella. Each tiny flower has 5 petals and gives off a subtle, slightly spicy fragrance when you get close.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms large, bushy clumps that can dominate a forest understory spot, with multiple thick stems rising from the ground. The overall silhouette is broad and leafy, almost shrub-like but entirely herbaceous.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Dark purple-black berries in rounded clusters that ripen in late summer, each berry about the size of a small pea. The berries have a sweet-spicy taste but are generally considered inedible raw.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, smooth stems that are often tinged with red or purple, especially at the joints where leaves attach. The stems feel sturdy and somewhat succulent when fresh.

habitat: Look for American spikenard in rich, moist woodland soils throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. It thrives in shaded areas with deep, fertile soil, often near streams or in ravines where leaf litter accumulates. You'll typically find it growing alongside other shade-loving plants like wild ginger, bloodroot, and various ferns.

seasonality.spring: Large compound leaves unfurl in late spring, creating dramatic foliage displays in woodland understories. The thick stems emerge from the ground and rapidly expand into their full bushy form.
seasonality.summer: White flower clusters bloom in mid to late summer, followed by green berries. This is peak identification season when both the massive leaves and distinctive flower/fruit clusters are visible.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to dark purple-black and leaves may turn yellow before dying back. The plant becomes less prominent as it prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent above ground, with only the thick underground roots surviving until spring. Look for dried stem bases and scattered berry remnants as clues to summer locations.

funFact: American spikenard's roots can live for decades and weigh up to 10 pounds, becoming so large and gnarled that early botanists sometimes mistook them for tree roots when digging them up!
confusionNotes: The huge compound leaves might be confused with elderberry, but elderberry is a woody shrub with stems that persist through winter, while spikenard dies back completely. Remember: "Spikenard disappears, elderberry stays here" - if you see woody stems in winter, it's not spikenard.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this plant with the biblical spikenard (Nardostachys jatamansi), which is an entirely different plant from the Himalayas. Early settlers gave our native plant this name because its roots were also aromatic and used medicinally, but they're not related species.
compareHints: American spikenard is much larger and more robust than its relatives - wild sarsaparilla stays close to the ground with leaves only 6-12 inches tall, while bristly sarsaparilla is covered in prickles. Devil's walkingstick has similar large leaves but is a woody shrub with fierce thorns covering its stems, unlike spikenard's smooth, herbaceous growth.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild sarsaparilla is much shorter than its Aralia relatives - bristly sarsaparilla grows taller with prickly stems, while American spikenard can reach 6 feet with multiple compound leaves and a more robust appearance.

Among New England's Aralia species, bristly sarsaparilla is the shortest and most rough-textured, preferring dry soils unlike wild sarsaparilla's forest preference or American spikenard's love of rich, moist areas.

Among its Aralia relatives in New England, Japanese angelica tree is by far the tallest and most tree-like, while wild sarsaparilla stays low to the ground and American spikenard is an herbaceous perennial.
Unlike its native New England Aralia cousins which are mostly low woodland herbs, Chinese angelica-tree grows much larger and lacks the thorns found on devil's walkingstick.
Among its Aralia relatives in New England, devil's walkingstick is unmistakable due to its woody, tree-like growth and extensive spines.
Japanese spikenard dwarfs its New England relatives like wild sarsaparilla and American spikenard, growing 2-3 times taller with much more robust stems.
